title: Halving a poll's margin
hook: A poll's margin of error is too wide. How many more people does it take to halve it?

doesNotKnow: how the margin of error scales with sample size

misconception: Doubling the sample halves the margin of error.
objective: The learner can explain that the margin shrinks with the square root of the sample size: 1,000 people give about 3.1 points, 2,000 only 2.2, and 4,000 (four times as many) 1.5.

claims.text: For a random poll of n people with support near 50%, the 95% margin of error is 1.96 x sqrt(0.25 / n): about 3.1 points at 1,000, 2.2 at 2,000 and 1.5 at 4,000, so the 4,000 band is half as wide as the dashed 1,000 band (the reveal opens only after a stop at 4,000).
claims.source: Normal approximation to the binomial; margin() in src/demos/probability/halve-the-margin-cost/model.ts gives 3.099, 2.191, 1.550 (also 6.2 at 250, 4.4 at 500, 1.1 at 8,000). | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check.

claims.text: About 95% of random polls land within the margin of error of the true value.
claims.source: Definition of the 95% margin (1.96 standard errors). The stage's seeded polls (seed 1936, untuned; a separate stream per size) put 95, 96, 95, 97, 95, 97 of 100 inside at 250, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 8,000.

claims.text: The margin shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so half the error costs four times the people.
The margin covers only random sampling luck, not people who refuse to answer or a biased list.
claims.source: AAPOR, Margin of Sampling Error / Credibility Interval statement: the margin of sampling error does not include non-response, coverage or measurement error.

recall.question: A survey of 500 people has a margin of about 4.4 points. Roughly how many people would bring it to about 2.2 points?
recall.why: Halving the margin takes four times the sample: 500 x 4 = 2,000. Doubling to 1,000 only reaches about 3.1.
